articles.body: Sponsored: This post is sponsored by UPDF. The testing, opinions and screenshots are my own. Why PDFs still matter in my workflow I write code for a living, yet a surprising amount of my week happens inside PDFs. Client contracts, invoices, API specs, research papers and technical documentation that only ships as a download all land in my inbox as PDFs. For years the default tool for this has been Adobe Acrobat, and for years it has felt like more software, and more subscription, than someone running a small development business really needs. articles.title: Why your OCR sees ID photos sideways: EXIF orientation, and fixing it with Pillow
articles.excerpt: A phone held upright doesn't rotate the pixels it saves. It stores the image in the camera sensor's orientation, often landscape, and adds an EXIF Orientation tag (value 6, for example, means "rotate…
articles.body: A phone held upright doesn't rotate the pixels it saves. It stores the image in the camera sensor's orientation , often landscape, and adds an EXIF Orientation tag (value 6, for example, means "rotate 90° clockwise to display"). Photo viewers and browsers apply the tag, so the user sees an upright document. OCR and face detection read the raw pixels , so they get the document sideways : text lines run vertically and recognition quality collapses. The fix is one line with Pillow, ImageOps.exif_transpose(img) , applied before anything else touches the image. It has to come first, because re-encoding or stripping metadata before applying it loses the orientation permanently . Tested Python below.
articles.author: Ali Ahmed

articles.title: Limiting concurrency in Python asyncio with a semaphore and per-task timeouts, in the right order
articles.excerpt: asyncio.gather(*(call(x) for x in items)) starts every call at once: with a thousand prompts, that's a thousand simultaneous requests to an LLM API, and an immediate wall of 429s. Cap it with asyncio.…
articles.body: asyncio.gather(*(call(x) for x in items)) starts every call at once : with a thousand prompts, that's a thousand simultaneous requests to an LLM API, and an immediate wall of 429s. Cap it with asyncio.Semaphore(n) : each task waits for a slot before it starts. Give each call a timeout with asyncio.timeout() , and pass return_exceptions=True so one failure doesn't cancel the rest. The order matters: the timeout must go inside the semaphore. Put it outside, and the clock starts while the task is still queueing, so tasks time out without ever running ; in my test, 8 of 10 did. Here's the correct version in a dozen lines, tested on Python 3.11 and later.

articles.excerpt: Originally published on the ApplyOS blog by Najib Oladosu, a software engineer based in Nigeria. An AI response can read well and still be attached to the wrong input. Imagine uploading a resume, chec…
articles.body: Originally published on the ApplyOS blog by Najib Oladosu, a software engineer based in Nigeria. An AI response can read well and still be attached to the wrong input. Imagine uploading a resume, checking it against a job description, then saving an edited version. When you return to the feedback screen, which version does that feedback describe? That question shaped how I built Job Fit in ApplyOS . The feature compares a saved resume with an application's job description. To make the feedback useful, I need to keep the result connected to the exact resume that went into the request. This article walks through the current implementation in Next.js, TypeScript and Supabase PostgreSQL. The screenshots use demonstration records. Their scores are examples, not hiring predictions.

articles.body: Grand Theft Auto 6 was released on Thursday, Nov. 19... officially. Millions of players around the world actually got to play it on Nov. 18 by moving to New Zealand. Well, not actually. Players just changed their account's region to New Zealand. It's a known trick that lets gamers access digital games before release when companies opt for a staggered launch, as with GTA 6 . Reports indicate that, in the UK and the US, 2 million Xbox players used the New Zealand trick to gain access to GTA 6 early. And that doesn't even account for the rest of the world or PlayStation players.

articles.title: Einstein was right! Scientists verify 1st image of a black hole ever captured
articles.excerpt: An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity, and that verifies Einstein's greatest theory.
articles.body: An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity. That, in turn, verifies Einstein's greatest theory, general relativity , which first predicted the existence of black holes and what their immediate surroundings would look like. Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image shows the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away. The image of this black hole , designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement. That may lead to the question: why did it need verifying at all?

articles.title: APOD: 2026 November 20 – V-G-R
articles.excerpt: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different im…
articles.body: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. V-G-R Explanation: On November 17, fans of interstellar spaceflight around planet Earth were invited to shine a message into the night sky. Traced by a flashlight beam switched on and off, the dashes and dots of a Morse code message captured in this time exposure from the Emirates Astronomical Observatory, are read V-G-R. That’s a call sign for the Voyager 1 spacecraft currently in interstellar space some 26 billion kilometers away.
